title: GLP-1 Palate Panel for Food R&D
one_liner: A managed panel of GLP-1 users and their households that food and restaurant companies rent to test products, portions and health claims.
customer: R&D and insights teams at mid-size CPG (protein, snacks, frozen), restaurant chain menu teams, foodservice for hospitals and senior living, and supplement brands that need claim substantiation ($25-150k per study).
problem: 73% of GLP-1 users report taste changes and 70% lose joy in eating, so 'just add protein' fails. About 70% change what the household eats, and non-users adopt 30-50% of the changes, so the affected base is ~50% larger than the user count. Food companies are reformulating and launching 'GLP-1 friendly' labels on general-population panels and conflicting forecasts.
solution: Recruit and maintain a segmented panel (drug, dose, weeks on therapy, aversion profile, household makeup). Run sensory, portion and format tests plus home-use tests and 8-12 week muscle and satiety claim studies. Deliver 'aversion maps' (which textures and smells trigger nausea at which dose) and household spillover models.
why_now: Households with a GLP-1 user doubled from ~11% to 22% in under 3 years. Pills launched in 2026 broaden the base. CPG is mid-reformulation, and FTC claim scrutiny makes 'evidence-backed' labels valuable. Purchase-panel incumbents see what is bought, not why.
revenue_model: $25-150k per study, plus $40-100k/year data subscription for 'aversion map' updates.
non_obvious_insight: The 'GLP-1 consumer' is 5-6 sensory segments that shift with dose and week on therapy, not one persona. Forecasting from sales data cannot separate them, but a panel can. The picks-and-shovels of a reformulation wave are the testers, not the brands.
first_30_days: Recruit 300 panelists from subreddits and Facebook groups with a $25 incentive, verified by photo of the pharmacy label. Publish a free 'taste change' survey report for press. Cold-email 30 CPG insights leads and land a first paid pilot of about $25k.

title: Thermal Safety Certification for Recovery Studios
one_liner: Staff certification, medication-aware intake screening and water-quality logging that insurers will soon require of sauna and cold-plunge operators.
customer: Contrast-therapy studios, gym recovery rooms, hotels and spas, paying monthly per location.
problem: Chain: studios are rolling out at speed (one brand added 25 locations in about 20 months and plans 100 more), so hundreds of new hires with no clinical training run 190F rooms and shared 40F tubs; customers increasingly take GLP-1s, blood-pressure meds or diuretics that raise fainting and dehydration risk; shared plunge water has no consistent standard and health departments are unsure how to classify it. One serious incident will trigger insurer exclusions and regulator attention.
solution: Three-part kit: a 90-minute 'Thermal Host' certification with annual refresh; tablet check-in screening (conditions and medications mapped to green/yellow/red session guidance plus waiver logging); and a water sensor pack (ORP, pH, chlorine, temperature) that auto-generates logs for inspectors and insurers.
why_now: The recovery boom (Nordic-style attendance up about 33 percent in 2025), mass GLP-1 use (about 1 in 8 adults), and no existing standard mean insurers and health departments are about to look for controls.
revenue_model: $99-199 per month per location, $39 per staff certification, sensor rental $49 per month per tub, plus insurer or broker referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: Be the standard before the incident: insurers would rather subsidize a certification than write exclusions, and the screening data is a wedge to premium programs. GLP-1 plus heat is the specific collision no one is training for.
first_30_days: Draft the protocol with a sports-medicine physician and a pool-operations consultant, sell it to 5 independent studios in one metro at a discounted founding rate, and ask two studio-focused insurance brokers for a premium credit for certified locations.

title: Muscle Ultrasound Scans as a Gym Vital Sign
one_liner: A five-minute, AI-read thigh ultrasound that tells GLP-1 users and lifters whether they are keeping their muscle.
customer: Gyms, GLP-1 and weight-loss clinics and PT clinics; consumers pay $29-49 per scan, clinics pay per-scan licenses.
problem: Studies suggest 20-50 percent of weight lost on GLP-1 drugs can be lean mass, but scales, bioimpedance and photos cannot show muscle and DEXA is costly and inconvenient. Trainers and clinics have no cheap, objective muscle metric to motivate clients or steer dosing and training.
solution: A coach scans the quadriceps with a handheld probe; AI segments rectus femoris and vastus intermedius thickness and echogenicity; results are trended over time and against a cohort. Positioned as general wellness muscle-thickness tracking that integrates with training and nutrition plans, not diagnosis.
why_now: Handheld ultrasound now shows excellent agreement with cart systems for quadriceps thickness (ICC above 0.9 in a 2025 study), automated AI muscle segmentation is maturing, muscle loss on GLP-1s was a headline debate at ADA 2026, and the FDA's wellness posture is looser.
revenue_model: $29-49 per scan retail; gym device-plus-software rental at $299-499 per month; per-scan fees for clinics.
non_obvious_insight: Trend in thickness, not absolute mass, is precise enough to change behavior. It is a retention and upsell tool for gyms (more strength coaching for people who can see the muscle they are protecting).
first_30_days: Buy two handheld probes, validate against DEXA on 50 volunteers with a partner clinic, run scan days at three gyms and one GLP-1 clinic at $39 per scan, and sign the first monthly device subscription.

title: Provider-in-Residence: Vacant Units Become Childcare
one_liner: Convert vacant ground-floor apartments in lease-up buildings into licensed family child care homes run by vetted early-educator residents, paid for out of the landlord's existing concession budget.
customer: Multifamily owners and operators in concession-heavy Sun Belt markets (success fee per activated unit), family child care entrepreneurs (a back-office subscription), and residents or subsidy programs paying tuition.
problem: Licensed capacity is barely growing (centers +1.5% and family homes +4.3% in 2024) while two children in center care cost more than rent in every state and the average childcare worker earns about $33,000. Meanwhile 1.2M apartment units are in lease-up, concessions run 15.8% of stabilized units (37% in Austin), it takes 34 days to lease, and owners are giving away free months on units that could earn nothing better.
solution: Pre-screen buildings for ground-floor 2-3 bedroom units that pass local family child care home rules (which in many states are treated as residential use). Recruit early educators, nannies and ex-teachers, fit out the unit (child-proofing, egress), coach them through licensing, and lease them the unit at a discount in place of the concession, so they live and work there. Resident families get priority. The operator handles enrollment, billing, subsidy paperwork, insurance and a shared substitute pool across buildings.
why_now: The lease-up glut has made concessions a real, measurable budget line and landlords are experimenting with anything that fills units or improves retention. The 2025-26 tax changes (DCFSA raised to $7,500, larger 45F credit) push employers and families toward childcare spending. Family child care homes are the fastest-growing licensed segment.
revenue_model: Landlord success fee of about $2-4K per activated unit (about one to two months of rent), 6-8% of tuition for back-office and subsidy handling, and a group insurance margin.
non_obvious_insight: A childcare seat is worth about $1,300 a month to a family, far more than a month of free rent is to a prospect, and a family with a child in the building is far less likely to move. The concession budget is already spent, and spending it on seats produces supply in a category where zoning is usually on your side.
first_30_days: Pick one metro with high concessions such as Austin, Phoenix, Atlanta or Nashville and check the state's family-home rules (ratios, floor level, egress). Pitch 5 lease-up operators and sign two letters of intent for 2-3 units each. Recruit three providers through early-educator communities and begin licensing, aiming for first enrollments by month four or five.

title: Remote Second-RN for Rural Night Shifts
one_liner: A pool of remote nurses that acts as the recorded, independent second person on video for narcotic waste, blood checks and high-alert drug double-checks when a rural hospital has three nurses on at 3am.
customer: Chief nursing officers and pharmacy directors at critical access hospitals (25 beds or fewer, roughly 1,300 in the US), plus the malpractice and captive insurers that cover them. Hospitals pay a monthly subscription.
problem: Policy requires a second licensed person to witness controlled-substance waste and to independently double-check insulin, heparin, blood and pediatric doses. At night at a rural hospital that second person is a nurse who is mid-code or mid-admission. Every nurse knows the witness signature is often given without actually watching. That is the most common way nurses divert drugs, and it is also how honest nurses end up with paper trails that would not survive an audit. The hospital cannot prove the witness happened. The other option is waking a colleague from another unit, which delays care.
solution: Start with a $150 tablet-and-camera cart at the dispensing cabinet. A remote RN appears on video within 60 seconds, watches the waste happen, and attests in a portal. The system keeps a time-stamped video clip and an audit log matched to the cabinet's waste records, exported as a PDF for the diversion committee. Then add two-RN blood transfusion verification, independent double-checks for high-alert drugs, and a 'second set of eyes' call for pediatric dosing. Do no EHR integration at first. Matching by timestamp is enough to sell.
why_now: The Bluesight 2026 State of Hospital Pharmacy report says about 63% of health-system leaders reported at least one diversion incident in the past year, and waste is a top diversion method because witnessing is loosely policed. Virtual nursing has become normal since 2024, and the Nurse Licensure Compact now covers most states, so one remote nurse can cover many hospitals. State Rural Health Transformation Program money is flowing, with every state having posted at least one funding opportunity by August 2026, and workforce and quality dollars can pay for this. Whether remote-video witnessing is acceptable is mostly a hospital-policy and pharmacy and therapeutics committee decision, but each state's board of pharmacy and nursing board should be checked before launch.
revenue_model: $1,500-2,500 per hospital per month, plus a per-event fee for transfusion and double-check calls above a set volume. A typical rural ED has 10-25 waste events a night at 2-3 minutes each, so one remote RN can cover roughly 8-12 hospitals per night. Estimated gross margin is 40-50%. A secondary revenue line is a discount arrangement with medical liability insurers, who benefit from the audit trail.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone selling diversion software (analytics, cabinet data mining, waste-testing) tries to detect diversion after the fact. Insiders know the root problem is that no real second person exists at night in a small hospital. You do not need better detection. You need to supply the missing colleague, cheaply and on camera. The service also protects honest nurses, who will therefore support it and not resist it.
first_30_days: Recruit 6 per-diem or retired RNs with compact licenses who want remote night hours at $35-40/hr. Use an off-the-shelf tablet with a recording app and a simple web portal that produces the PDF log. Offer free 30-day pilots to two critical access hospitals through the founder nurse's own pharmacy director and CNO. Get the pilot approved as a policy amendment at the pharmacy and therapeutics committee. Convert to a $1,500 monthly contract after 30 days if the audit log is shown to the diversion committee and the hospital's insurer.

title: White-Label Camera Forensics for Cities and Schools
one_liner: Scan municipal and school camera, recorder and IoT fleets to unmask white-labeled hardware with covered Hikvision or Dahua internals and produce grant-ready compliance attestations and phased replacement plans.
customer: City and county IT and police departments, school districts, transit agencies and the MSPs and integrators serving them. They pay $3-15k per fleet audit plus an annual monitoring fee.
problem: Federal grant terms (DOJ, DHS and FEMA, school-safety programs) bar covered surveillance equipment under NDAA Section 889 and 2 CFR 200.216, including where it is a substantial or essential component of a system sold under another brand. Many fleets bought 2015-2020 contain OEM boards nobody can trace, and the integrator who sold them has a conflict in saying so. Sensor stacking (noise detectors on license-plate readers) is spreading while surveillance-vendor scrutiny grows.
solution: An agentless scanner that fingerprints devices by firmware, banners, MAC ranges and cloud endpoints (including peer-to-peer relay services) to reveal OEM lineage across cameras, NVRs, access panels and doorbells. Output is an asset inventory, a grant-attestation letter, and a replacement plan sequenced against grant cycles, with domestic or trade-compliant alternatives. Integrators pay a referral fee for replacement work.
why_now: Compliance is now BOM-level across industries, and grant conditions are being enforced more tightly. Cities face ADA Title II (Apr 2027) and CJIS 6.0 (Oct 2027) deadlines that already force IT audits. Public backlash over camera vendors makes proof of diligence politically valuable.
revenue_model: $3-15k per fleet audit, $1-3 per device per year for monitoring and re-scan, and 3-8% referral fees on replacement projects. Sell through MSPs and state cooperative contracts.
non_obvious_insight: Compliance is defined by the chip in the box, not the label on the box. Origin lineage of white-labeled OEM electronics is an unpriced supply-chain data problem that only shows up at the moment a city touches federal money, and the fingerprint database becomes the moat.
first_30_days: Release a free 'Is my camera a Hikvision?' desktop scanner for IT staff as lead-gen, audit 3 school districts at cost to build the fingerprint set, and then sell $5k audits to the first 5 districts via grant writers and state school-safety offices.

title: Identical Object Kits for Robot Data Farms
one_liner: Manufacture and ship standardized kits of hundreds of everyday-object variants, panels of handles, hinges and knobs, and task fixtures, so that every home and lab collecting robot training data uses the same physical objects.
customer: Robot-learning startups and university labs, and the data-collection vendors that run gig-worker networks who record household demonstrations for humanoid and manipulation models.
problem: At-home robot data collection is booming, but contributors use whatever cups, jars and cabinet handles they own. That makes data hard to compare, hard to control for variation and impossible to replicate across sites. A robot learning to open a drawer needs the same drawer types in 500 places.
solution: A 'Kitchen-100' kit: 100 standardized, individually scanned objects (cups, lids, jars, tongs, utensils, packages), plus modular handle, hinge, latch and knob panels and drawer or door fixtures with known mass, friction and geometry. Ship to thousands of contributors and to labs. Sell new object sets monthly so datasets keep growing coherently, and bundle the digital twins (scans and physics parameters) for simulation.
why_now: Humanoid and robot-foundation-model companies are competing for training data in 2026, and coverage such as MIT Technology Review's April 2026 report on gig workers training humanoids at home shows the supply chain for that data is still improvised. Only a handful of vendors can collect at scale, and none owns the standardized physical layer.
revenue_model: Kit sales ($150 to $600 each in batches of hundreds or thousands), monthly new-object subscriptions, custom fixture builds for labs ($5k to $50k) and licensing of scan and physics data.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck for physical AI is not only more demonstrations but controlled, comparable ones. Whoever ships the same 100 objects to 5,000 kitchens gets a natural experiment in robot learning, and the kit sets the de facto benchmark. Old benchmarks (like a single reference set of household objects) are small and dated, so a manufacturing-scale, refreshable standard can become infrastructure.
first_30_days: Design and print or source a v0 kit of 50 to 100 objects and a set of handle panels. Scan each object and publish a free open dataset as marketing. Pitch 15 labs and 5 data-collection vendors with a pilot offer: 20 kits at cost plus a custom object of their choice. Target one vendor pilot of 200 kits.

title: Pet Sitters as Home-Energy Field Workforce
one_liner: A trained, insured network of pet sitters and dog walkers who already hold house keys and midday access, performing unlicensed home-energy tasks that stall electrification programs.
customer: VPP and DR aggregators, utility weatherization and heat pump programs, and home-battery/heat-pump installers that pay per completed visit ($40-90). Homeowners see it as free or discounted enrollment.
problem: Electricians are scarce (about 81,000 openings a year) and data centers pay 25-30% premiums, so home electrification loses labor. But many program stalls are not licensed work: 'customer must be home' no-shows, devices offline, thermostat and smart-plug swaps, filter changes, weatherstripping, photos for interconnection paperwork, and plug-in solar setup. Each one is a truck roll priced like an electrician's.
solution: Recruit and background-check pet sitters and walkers, insure them, and train them on about a dozen no-license tasks with guided QR workflows. Schedule tasks alongside pet visits, with the owner's explicit opt-in and strict limits (plug-in and low-voltage only, no panel work). Route orders from utilities, VPP operators and installers, and include placement of pet-zone sensors where relevant.
why_now: Data-center wage arbitrage is draining electricians (one report shows $20 to $35 an hour), 25C/25D subsidies ended so programs are cutting cost per home, and at least nine states have signed plug-in solar laws (around 1.2 kW, UL 3700 exists), which makes non-electrician installs legal and needed.
revenue_model: Per-visit fee billed to the program ($40-90) with 25-35% margin after sitter pay, training and certification fees, and a subscription for large programs that need a managed scheduling and QA layer.
non_obvious_insight: The energy transition's shortage is not just electricians. A large slice of tasks need access and trust rather than a license, and pet sitters uniquely hold both, visit on a schedule, and are a labor pool data centers cannot poach.
first_30_days: Pick one metro where a local sitter collective or Rover/Wag-heavy sitter community exists. Recruit and train 20 sitters on 5 tasks (thermostat, smart plug, offline-device reconnect, filter swap, plug-in solar setup). Sell a pilot at $60/visit to one co-op or heat-pump installer needing post-install commissioning and connectivity fixes. Confirm liability coverage before the first visit.

title: Regulatory Slip Desk for Compliance Budget Decisions
one_liner: A probability-weighted deadline desk that tells compliance heads which rules will probably slip, which will not, and which controls are worth building now regardless.
customer: GCs, heads of compliance and CFOs at companies with $200M-$20B revenue facing many regimes at once (EU AI Act, CBAM, CRA, CSRD, US state privacy and AI laws). Secondary buyers are compliance-software vendors timing their sales and investors betting on delay.
problem: Deadlines have become unreliable. AI Act high-risk duties moved to 2 Dec 2027 (Annex III) and 2 Aug 2028 (Annex I) per the tracker (the Omnibus status is unverified), CSRD waves 2 and 3 slipped to 2028, while CBAM and CRA reporting did not move. Teams either overspend on rules that later slip or get blindsided by rules that hold. Law-firm alerts explain what a rule says, not whether it will arrive on time.
solution: A subscription tracker of about 100 obligations, each with the hard date, a written probability of further slip or scope cut with reasons (trilogue calendar, standards readiness, member-state transposition, litigation), and a split between 'no-regret controls' that satisfy several regimes (inventories, logging, supplier data) and 'wait for clarity' items. Trigger alerts ('if standard X is not cited by date Y, slip probability rises'). A public scored track record of every past forecast, plus a quarterly board memo.
why_now: 2025-26 was the year of delays and unwinds: the Digital Omnibus reshuffled AI Act dates, CSRD got stop-the-clock, and several US rules were dropped or vacated (background, verify). Buyers have now been burned in both directions.
revenue_model: $12-40k/year per enterprise seat pack, a $3k/year SME tier sold via newsletter, and a data feed to compliance-software vendors at $30-100k.
non_obvious_insight: Compliance is an options problem, not a deadline problem. Insiders sell obligations as fixed; the value is pricing probability and timing and finding multi-regime no-regret work. A public forecast track record is a moat law firms will not build because they cannot afford to be visibly wrong.
first_30_days: Publish a free 'Slip Index' showing the base rate of deadline moves across the 30 largest EU and US digital rules since 2023. Build a 500-person newsletter via IAPP-style and LinkedIn communities, and pre-sell 10 annual subscriptions at a $6k founder price with a money-back guarantee. Make every forecast in writing with a date.

title: Parametric Recovery Cover for Tourism Towns
one_liner: Annual parametric policies bought by destination tourism boards that pay out within days when fire, smoke, flood or road closures crater visitor demand, even with no physical damage.
customer: Destination marketing organizations and county or city tourism authorities in single-access, hazard-exposed resort towns (Estes Park, Truckee/Tahoe, Big Bear, Gatlinburg, Outer Banks, Asheville, Maui), funded by lodging taxes (transient occupancy tax, TOT) with $50-500K premium budgets.
problem: Business-interruption cover requires physical damage, and civil-authority riders are short. After Lahaina, Asheville and Caldor, the losses came from closed roads, smoke and perception, not damaged hotels. TOT revenue funds recovery marketing and services, and it collapses exactly when the town most needs to advertise. Retail insurers are retreating from these towns and small lodging and restaurants cannot buy adequate cover.
solution: We design tourism-specific indices and place the cover. Triggers use hazard evidence (evacuation orders, AQI days over threshold, DOT road-closure days) confirmed by an occupancy drop versus baseline (STR/hotel data such as AirDNA). Payout scales are calibrated to historical TOT dips. The policyholder is the DMO, which re-grants through its existing marketing and small-business grant programs. Capacity comes from a fronting carrier or parametric MGA plus reinsurers and ILS. We deliver index design, backtests, placement and the claims data oracle.
why_now: Reinsurance is softening fast: Howden reports property-cat risk-adjusted rates down up to 25% at 1 June 2026 after -16% and -14.7% earlier, with record capital (about $790B, secondary source). Niche capacity is now cheap while retail carriers still retreat. Cat bond issuance hit records in H1 2026 (about $18B). Travel booking windows are about 33 days, so a fast cash-funded comeback campaign can restore bookings quickly.
revenue_model: Broker/MGA-style commission of 12-18% of premium, plus index licensing and annual re-modeling fees. Ten towns at about $150K average premium and 15% commission is roughly $225K in year one, scaling through state travel associations.
non_obvious_insight: Tourism loss after disasters is mostly access and perception, not damage. A public tourism board is the rare buyer that can purchase parametric cover and redistribute it to small businesses that could never qualify individually. The lodging-tax series is a clean, public, monthly loss history no adjuster touched. Public-entity buyers also sidestep the homeowner rate-filing regime that strangles retail products.
first_30_days: Backtest four past events (East Troublesome/Estes Park 2020, Caldor/Tahoe 2021, Lahaina 2023, Helene/Asheville 2024) using public TOT reports, AQI and road-closure logs. Produce 'what you would have received' one-pagers. Pitch 10 DMO executive directors and 3 state travel associations. Get a parametric MGA or fronting partner to quote. Target the first bound policy in the spring 2027 budget and fire-season renewal window.

title: AI Provenance Audits for Game IP Deals
one_liner: Due-diligence audits, plus a signed process-capture plugin, that tell publishers and acquirers what in a game is verifiably human-made and what IP they actually own.
customer: Small and mid publishers, game aggregators and acquirers, and lenders (idea 1's future competitors). Festival and award organizers pay for finalist verification. They pay $1.5-6k per audit. Studios and freelance artists pay $0-199 for the evidence pack.
problem: Steam's AI disclosure is self-attested. In January 2026 the form was narrowed to player-facing generative content. About one in five store listings now disclose AI use, and players punish undisclosed use, including refund fights over late disclosure. The US Copyright Office position is that purely AI-generated material isn't copyrightable, so a publisher buying a game with heavy AI art owns thinner IP than the price assumes. Awards bodies have reversed honors after discovering AI use.
solution: Two parts. First, a local plugin set (Aseprite, Krita, Blender, Photoshop, plus git and Perforce hooks, and C2PA where available) writes a tamper-evident, timestamped hash chain of authoring events, with no screen recording. Second, an audit desk takes a shipped build and repo and produces an asset-by-asset provenance map: evidenced human, AI-assisted, or unknown. It adds a Steam-disclosure recommendation and a copyrightability memo prepared with counsel.
why_now: Valve's January 2026 form rewrite left studios unsure what counts. AI use is now mainstream (roughly 20% of listings) and controversial. Awards and festivals are getting burned. Publishers are adding AI warranties to contracts and want a way to verify them.
revenue_model: Per-audit fees, bulk pricing for publishers with catalogs, a per-finalist fee for festivals and awards, and a paid studio subscription for evidence-pack export. Artists get the credential free, which builds the network.
non_obvious_insight: Classifiers run on shipped assets are unreliable, and false positives on human artists are reputational poison. The only defensible evidence is process metadata captured at creation, which is nearly impossible to reconstruct afterward. So the buyer is the balance-sheet buyer who cares about IP ownership, not the player. Freelancers who want a 'verified human' credential to win commissions pull the tool into studios from below.
first_30_days: Hand-sell audits: contact 30 small publishers and aggregators, and do 3 discounted audits by reading source-control history and interviewing the team. Ship a minimal Aseprite or Krita plus git capture plugin. Pitch two indie festivals or awards on verifying their finalists. Publish an anonymized 'what audits usually find' write-up.

title: Pickleball Noise Measurement Standard and Monitoring
one_liner: A court-defensible protocol, sensor kit and certification for measuring pickleball noise, sold to towns, HOAs and clubs.
customer: Parks and planning departments, HOAs, private clubs, court builders and municipal attorneys.
problem: Paddle impacts read roughly 70-80 dBA at 15 ft against 40-55 dBA ambient, and disputes are closing or limiting courts. In April 2026 a Missouri judge voided Kirkwood's restrictions as 'arbitrary, capricious and invalid' because noise could not be consistently measured. That leaves cities, clubs and neighbors all without an enforceable standard.
solution: A measurement protocol for impulsive, tonal sports noise (peak and Leq metrics, distance and background correction), a calibrated ~$500 sensor kit with cloud reporting and automatic compliance reports, expert-witness-ready PDFs, and an 'approved low-impact site' certification that helps at permit hearings. Add mitigation advice (barriers, quiet paddles and balls).
why_now: The Kirkwood ruling and hundreds of local ordinance fights, with participation at 24.3M and rising.
revenue_model: Kit sale or rental ($500 plus $30/month monitoring), $2-5k per-site certification, $1.5k expert reports, and protocol licensing to municipalities.
non_obvious_insight: Noise fights are fights over measurement. Whoever supplies the trusted protocol becomes the referee both sides must use, and courts have already said unmeasurable ordinances fail.
first_30_days: Contact 10 town attorneys and HOA boards currently in noise disputes and offer loaner sensor rigs. Publish an open draft protocol with an acoustical-engineer advisor. Aim for the first paid report in month one.

title: Celebration-of-Life Halls in Closed Churches
one_liner: Lease shuttered churches and run them as turnkey memorial venues sold at checkout by direct-cremation providers and hospices.
customer: Families holding a memorial after a cremation ($2.5-6k per event). Referral partners are low-cost and direct-cremation providers, hospice social workers and estate attorneys.
problem: Cremation was about 62% of US dispositions in 2024 and is projected to hit ~82% by 2045. Direct cremation is the fastest-growing category, but it unbundles the ceremony. Families end up planning a memorial themselves in a restaurant or backyard, funeral-home chapels are being sold off, and nobody runs the day: music, slideshow, live-stream, seating, catering, display of ashes.
solution: Take a long lease or lease-to-own on a closed church. Denominations often discount buildings for gentle uses and restrict bars or clubs, so a memorial hall is an easy yes. Install AV and live-streaming for far-away family, and hire a bereavement-trained coordinator. Add a photo-to-memorial-video service, caterer partnerships and a wall of memory. Sell it as a $2,900 'Add a Celebration of Life' package on the partner's checkout page. The other six days a week, book weddings, concerts and community events. Columbarium niches are a phase-two option after legal review.
why_now: Direct-cremation startups have marketing reach and no physical venues. Congregations keep closing after COVID. Live-stream AV and AI-assisted photo-to-video tools are now cheap enough for a two-person team to run.
revenue_model: Event package fee (venue, AV, coordinator; $2.5-6k). Catering margin. Memorial video upsell (~$400). Referral revenue share to partners. Weekday event rentals. Later, columbarium niches with perpetual-care fees.
non_obvious_insight: The direct-cremation revolution unbundled the ceremony and nobody rebundled it. A sanctuary already has the emotional weight and acoustics, and resale restrictions make sellers accept a low price for a respectful use. Idle-week rental income turns a grief business into a resilient one.
first_30_days: Contact diocesan and conference property offices about 5 closed churches for month-to-month special-use agreements. Pilot 3 events at cost-plus with 2 direct-cremation providers and 2 hospices. Collect testimonials and photos. Stand up a booking page and a bereavement-friendly phone concierge.

title: Solar Closing Desk for Listing Agents
one_liner: A per-listing service that clears solar leases, PPAs, loans and UCC-1 fixture filings before the house hits the MLS, so escrow does not blow up in week three.
customer: Listing agents, brokerages and title/escrow firms in solar-dense counties (CA, AZ, FL, TX, NJ, MA, CO, NV, HI). The seller pays $395-795 per listing at closing from proceeds, or a brokerage pays a flat subscription.
problem: Solar lease and PPA transfers need provider consent, which can add 2-6 weeks to escrow and sometimes fails. Solar UCC-1 fixture filings show up on the title prelim and block closings, refinances and HELOCs. Agents usually discover this on day 20 of escrow, when the buyer's credit check fails or the provider's transfer queue stalls. One industry cite claims about half of agents have had solar complicate a deal. The 2015-2020 lease vintages are now entering resale years, and TPO is the only route to a federal credit since 2026, so volume rises for a decade.
solution: Start the clock at listing, not at contract. Within 48 hours, identify who owns the system using permit data, UCC search, the title prelim and a monitoring-account check. Order the provider's payoff and transfer packet. Soft-pre-qualify likely buyers in the provider's portal. Produce a one-page Solar Fact Sheet for the MLS with verified production history, remaining term, escalator and buyout cost. Then run the chosen path: payoff and UCC-3 termination, transfer with consent, or subordination to the new mortgage. Provide escrow instructions and agent scripts, and offer buyout financing through a partner.
why_now: TPO has become the dominant way to buy solar after 25D ended. First-wave lease systems are hitting the resale market, provider servicing is in flux after the Sunnova and SunPower failures (successor servicer SunStrong), and title companies are seeing more fixture-filing holds. Home sales are slow, so agents cannot afford failed escrows.
revenue_model: Flat per-listing fee paid at closing. Referral fee from lease-buyout lenders (about 1% of buyout). White-label subscription for title and escrow companies. Later, sell aggregated solar-adjustment data to appraisers and mortgage investors.
non_obvious_insight: Every provider's transfer team is a queue with known choke points: the buyer's credit pull, the time-limited buyer acceptance window, and UCC-3 termination filing lag. An installer sees this because neighbors' failed sales kill sales for the next solar rep. The fix is operational, not legal. Agents cannot price a lease because they cannot read production guarantees or escalators, so a plain fact sheet makes the solar a selling point instead of a discount.
first_30_days: Interview 15 listing agents in one solar-heavy county. Offer 5 active solar listings handled free in exchange for testimonials. Hire a part-time escrow officer or paralegal. Publish a Solar Home Sale Checklist for agents to get inbound leads. Sign a pilot with two local title companies. Use manual processes and one shared spreadsheet, with no software build until 50 listings.

title: Compute-Heated Housing: GPUs as the Boiler Room
one_liner: Put a liquid-cooled AI rack in an apartment tower's mechanical room and use its waste heat as the building's hot-water plant, cutting utility costs while hosting power-starved compute.
customer: Owners of 200-500 unit towers or planned conversions with central hot-water plants, especially in cities with building-emissions caps, paired with inference and neocloud operators seeking power and cooling.
problem: 20.7% of renters cannot pay utilities in full, gas boilers face per-ton fines under building-performance laws (NYC Local Law 97 tightens in 2030), and AI compute is starved for sites with power and cooling.
solution: Install one direct-liquid-cooled rack (about 100-130 kW) in the mechanical room. Capture waste heat, lift it with heat pumps to domestic hot water, and sell the building heat at a discount to gas or provide it free in exchange for hosting. The compute operator pays colocation rent, and we own design, integration and the thermal contract. Later expand to space heating and whole conversions.
why_now: Dense liquid-cooled racks produce capturable heat, AI power scarcity is acute, heat-pump hot water is mature, and building-emissions caps are tightening.
revenue_model: Heat-as-a-service at 30-40% of avoided energy cost, hosting margin share, and $25-50K design fees per building.
non_obvious_insight: By rough engineering estimate, a 300-unit building's average hot-water load (about 100-120 kW thermal) roughly equals one AI rack's heat output. The boiler room can host compute that cannot be sited elsewhere, and hot-water demand never sleeps. Precedents exist in Europe (data-furnace heaters and pool heating).
first_30_days: Run feasibility on five NYC and Chicago buildings with emissions-cap exposure. Get a letter of intent from one inference host for a 100 kW pilot. Sell three paid feasibility studies at $10-15K and line up host-funded pilot capex.

title: Flight simulator drills for county SNAP eligibility workers
one_liner: Short daily drills using synthetic cases built from the state's own error taxonomy, sold to county social-services directors who are about to pay for every eligibility mistake.
customer: County social services / DSS directors and supervisors in county-administered SNAP states (NY, NC, CA, OH, MN, CO, VA) and the state associations of counties. Buyers pay $12k-25k per county per year, or $150-300 per worker. States can buy statewide at $150k-500k.
problem: H.R.1 raises the state/county share of SNAP administrative costs from 50% to 75% starting October 2026. From October 2027, states with payment error rates of 6% or higher must pay part of benefit costs. In New York, St. Lawrence County faces an extra $776,000 in year one, Jefferson County over $1 million and Warren County $415,000. The state's error rate is 13% against a 6% line, a penalty of about $1B statewide, described as 'a missile heading right at New York State'. North Carolina's error rate is 6.69%, with state cost-share exposure of about $140M at 5% and $420M at 15%. The state's advice to counties is 'documenting, documenting, documenting'.
solution: A 15-minute daily micro-drill for eligibility workers: a synthetic household case (pay stubs, shelter costs, household composition changes, address changes) with a realistic case-file packet, where the worker computes eligibility and benefit. The drill feeds back the exact error that federal QC would cite. Cases are generated from the state's policy manual and the public USDA QC error categories (wage reporting, household size, address changes and shelter deductions are the common ones), with no real client data. Supervisors see per-worker error-type heatmaps and a coaching queue. Later: an optional second-look review desk staffed by former QC reviewers that samples a county's real closed cases.
why_now: The error-rate look-back, cost-shift start (October 2026) and penalty tiers (October 2027) create a hard two-year clock. Louisiana is paying cash bonuses to error spotters, Kansas hired an outside consultant, Virginia is buying technology for error checking, and NC is running monthly QC webinars and targeting high-error counties. States are visibly buying error-reduction help, and there is no standard product for it.
revenue_model: Per-worker annual subscription ($150-300) or flat per-county fee ($12k-25k); statewide contracts through the state SNAP office or county association; add-on per-case second-look review at $18-30/case.
non_obvious_insight: A county with a 0% error rate is still penalized if the state averages above 6%, so no county can solve this alone and the real buyer is the state or the association pooling county money. Meanwhile individual county directors are hurting now and have discretionary admin budgets and training budgets they can spend without an RFP. Synthetic cases avoid the PII and system-access barrier that blocks most govtech vendors in benefits programs, so a small team can start selling in weeks, not after a FedRAMP-style review. Evidence: county exposure and 13% New York error rate (https://www.northcountrypublicradio.org/news/story/53929/20260910/snap-cost-shift-pushes-north-country-counties-into-a-financial-bind); NC official on documentation, targeted training and CQI (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/9949745/north-carolina/executive/organizations/state-departments-and-agencies/mental-health/developmental-disabilities-and-substance-abuse-services/state-official-urges-counties-to-cut-snap-payment-error-rate-to-avoid-hr1-cost-shares); state remediation tactics such as bonuses, outside consultants and new training (https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/states-scramble-cut-snap-error-214614305.html).
first_30_days: Build 40 synthetic cases across the top error elements from one state's manual, with a scoring engine. Approach the state county association's SNAP resource group and 5 county DSS directors with a free 30-day pilot with a pre/post test on 10 new hires. Publish a 'your error rate in dollars' calculator for county commissioners. Convert the two most engaged counties to paid annual plans priced below their discretionary-purchase limits.

title: Market Rulebook Red Team for New Venues
one_liner: Turn a trading venue's plain-English rulebook into an executable model, then use adversarial agents to find manipulation exploits and propose rule patches before real attackers do.
customer: Operators of new or small marketplaces: CFTC-registered event-contract and prediction-market venues, tokenized-asset and crypto exchanges, carbon-credit registries, energy and capacity market operators, GPU-compute spot exchanges, and ad-auction platforms.
problem: Modern electronic markets are built for speed and transparency, which has 'created new attack surfaces and systemic risks', and they 'can be manipulated in ways unanticipated by their designers'. Venues test their matching engine software, but nobody systematically tests the market rules themselves (settlement sources, auction tie-breaks, position limits, fee rebates) for exploits. Regulators expect venues to show their contracts and rules resist manipulation, but there is no standard way to prove it.
solution: An agent pipeline. Step 1: an LLM converts the rulebook or tariff PDF into a formal mechanism spec (order types, matching rules, settlement, fees). Step 2: an agent-based simulator with attacker agents searches for profitable manipulation strategies (wash trading, spoofing and layering, oracle or settlement-source attacks, self-dealing through fee rebates, cross-market squeezes). Step 3: it proposes rule patches and re-runs the attacks as regression tests. Deliver a fuzz report and a CI-style re-run whenever the rules change.
why_now: DARPA's Intrinsic Market Resilience (IMR) program, with a proposers day October 1, 2026, abstracts due October 22 and proposals due December 7, 2026, explicitly bets that LLM automation plus rigorous modeling can automatically model market designs, find weaknesses and recommend repairs. New event-contract, tokenized and compute markets are launching faster than their rulebooks can be reviewed. LLMs only recently became good enough at turning long legal text into formal specs.
revenue_model: $25k to $60k fixed-price rulebook audit. $3k to $8k per month for continuous re-testing when rules or fee schedules change. Possible subcontract or teaming revenue on DARPA IMR or follow-on federal work.
non_obvious_insight: A rulebook is code that nobody compiles. DARPA is paying to build the compiler-plus-fuzzer, and the same tool works on any venue, so the government-funded R&D is a free market validation of the product category. The IMR page states the problem ('manipulated in ways unanticipated by their designers'), names markets from 'equities and bonds to energy and cloud computing resources', and describes the LLM-plus-formal-modeling approach: https://www.darpa.mil/research/programs/intrinsic-market-resilience-imr. Caveat: the public page names no specific exploits and says nothing about commercial adoption, so the private-sector demand (for example the CFTC's requirement that contracts not be readily susceptible to manipulation) is my inference from background knowledge, not from the DARPA page.
first_30_days: Pick 3 public rulebooks or tariffs (a new prediction-market venue, a public energy market tariff, a carbon registry methodology). Run the pipeline and publish 3 short teardown posts showing a concrete exploit and a patch. Email the compliance and product heads of 30 newly launched venues with their own teardown. Sell 2 fixed-price audits at $25k. In parallel, submit an abstract by October 22 or offer teaming to IMR prime bidders.

title: Add Megawatt-Hours to Already-Interconnected Batteries
one_liner: The queue limits megawatts, not megawatt-hours, so sell cheap add-on energy blocks to existing 2-hour battery and solar sites that already own the grid connection.
customer: Owners of 2019-2024 vintage 2-hour storage and solar sites (IPPs, infrastructure funds, utilities) in PJM, ERCOT and CAISO. Storage developers and data center developers who lack queue positions are the second buyer group.
problem: New MW wait years in interconnection queues. Stationary packs fell 45% to about $70/kWh and new projects average 3.5 hours. Existing 2-hour fleets are under-accredited for capacity, and their owners are not thinking about bolt-on energy.
solution: Engineer and finance duration uplift by adding DC-coupled or AC-block MWh behind the existing inverters and point of interconnection. Provide standardized BMS integration and warranty tooling. Second product: use surplus interconnection headroom at solar and wind farms to add storage MW, with a revenue share to the site owner. The company screens sites from public data, packages them and sells them or builds them.
why_now: Cell prices collapsed. Capacity prices at the cap reward accredited duration. Regulators (surplus interconnection service, MISO ERAS, PJM RRI) are openly trying to reuse existing grid connections.
revenue_model: Engineering and development fee per kWh added, a share of incremental capacity revenue, or resale of ready-to-build projects.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is the interconnection agreement, not the battery. Every existing 2-hour battery is a queue position with half its energy potential unused, and it is the one capacity addition that skips the queue.
first_30_days: List ~200 US storage projects at 2 hours or less from EIA-860 and ISO data. Model uplift economics for 10 of them under PJM and ERCOT rules. Send owners a one-page 'what two more hours earns you' analysis. Sign two or three paid feasibility studies. Line up a non-FEOC DC block supplier.

title: SNAP Rules Engine for Independent Grocers
one_liner: An API and POS plug-in that classifies every UPC against each state's changing SNAP soda and candy rules.
customer: Independent grocers and convenience stores in states with SNAP restrictions, and the POS and EBT vendors that serve them.
problem: 22 states have SNAP soda and candy restrictions in effect or pending, definitions differ by state, and a June 2026 ruling (Aragon v. Rollins) blocked waivers in five states, so rules keep flipping.
solution: A maintained UPC-level eligibility database by state and effective date, delivered as a POS plug-in and API with audit logs for SNAP authorization defense.
why_now: Patchwork state waivers and court reversals in 2026 mean retailers carry compliance liability without product-level data.
revenue_model: $30-60 per store per month, plus license fees from POS vendors.
non_obvious_insight: Court-driven rule flips make this a recurring data subscription rather than a one-time setup, and the liability sits with retailers who have no tooling.
first_30_days: Classify the top 5,000 UPCs for four states, pilot in 20 independent stores and one POS vendor, and set up a rule-change alert feed.

title: Immigration Deadline Sentinel for Work-Permit Households
one_liner: The wealthy keep immigration counsel on retainer to calendar, file early and bridge gaps; for $20/mo, give H-4, OPT, asylum-applicant and DACA households an encrypted deadline vault and family-readiness plan.
customer: Households whose work authorization depends on renewable USCIS documents: H-4/L-2 spouses with EADs, F-1 OPT/STEM OPT students, asylum applicants, DACA recipients, and pending adjustment applicants. Sold at $20/mo per household, or $4-8 per head through employers, university international offices, credit unions and churches.
problem: DHS ended automatic 540-day EAD extensions for renewals filed on or after 30 October 2025. USCIS advises filing up to 180 days early, yet some I-765 categories are reported at many months to a year or more, so gaps in work authorization mean lost jobs, licenses and health coverage. Rich families' lawyers prevent this by tracking every date; ordinary families rely on memory and WhatsApp.
solution: An end-to-end-encrypted vault, on-device where possible: photograph an EAD, I-94 or I-797 and it extracts dates and builds a household calendar (EAD file window opening at day 180, AR-11 address change within 10 days, OPT unemployment day counter, I-751, N-400 windows, passport expiries). It pre-fills renewal packets for attorney review, generates employer bridging letters, and monitors case status. For cases outside normal processing times it prepares a congressional-inquiry package. It adds a family-readiness plan (power of attorney, standby guardianship for children, contact tree, know-your-rights card). Flat-fee referrals go to attorneys and DOJ-accredited representatives. It is software and documents, not legal advice.
why_now: The October 2025 interim final rule ended automatic extensions, processing times are long, USCIS moved to a new I-765 form version (mandatory from March 2026), and enforcement anxiety is high in 2026. Employers and universities are scrambling to protect workers.
revenue_model: $20/mo per household; $3-6 per employee per month for employer or university dashboards; flat referral fees from partner attorneys; enterprise HR reporting tier.
non_obvious_insight: Wealthy people's immigration counsel adds most of its value before a crisis, by calendaring, filing early and pre-drafting backups, which software can supply for a fraction of the cost. Privacy-by-design (end-to-end encryption so a subpoena or breach yields nothing) is not just compliance but the differentiator for a population that fears data exposure. The paying wedge is the professional H-4/OPT segment and their employers, not the most vulnerable households.
first_30_days: Build a WhatsApp and spreadsheet MVP that ingests document photos and sends reminders. Partner with 2 immigration attorneys on flat-fee referral, 3 university international offices, and H-4 spouse and OPT Facebook groups. Enroll 100 households free, convert to $20/mo, and pilot with one employer HR team.

title: Pay-on-Close Homebuyer Readiness for Builders
one_liner: A builder-funded coaching and underwriting-repair program for the roughly half of showroom visitors who cannot yet qualify, paid per closing instead of through rate buydowns.
customer: Production and regional builders and their affiliated mortgage companies. The builder pays $2,000-$5,000 per attributable closing.
problem: Lennar says nearly 50% of visitors in many markets cannot immediately qualify for a mortgage, and it gives about 12% of price in incentives on a $372K average price, or roughly $45K per home. KB Home's cancellation rate is 18% of gross orders (up from 17%), and it makes 'minor adjustments' to keep buyers qualified. Builders spend heavily on lowering the monthly payment and almost nothing on fixing the reasons buyers fail underwriting.
solution: A 60-120 day cohort program runs alongside the builder's sales funnel for prospects who fail pre-qualification. It has four parts: (1) debt-to-income triage with a plan to pay down or restructure the few accounts that cause most failures, (2) lender-coordinated rapid rescoring, (3) co-borrower matching and down-payment-assistance navigation across state housing finance agencies, employer housing programs and gift rules, and (4) rent and utility payment reporting. Milestones are shared with the builder's lender through a dashboard. The vendor is paid only when a buyer the program touched closes on a home in the builder's community.
why_now: Mortgage rates are rising again (Paychex references a recent 25 bp Fed increase), and Lennar says rate-buydown costs are climbing. Resale inventory is at a decade high and is competing directly with new homes. KB Home's Executive Chairman says pricing is declining in more markets. The cheapest lever left is converting buyers who are near qualification.
revenue_model: $2,000-$5,000 success fee per closed home attributable to a program participant. Optional $300 per enrolled prospect for the coaching workload, credited against the success fee. Lender referral fees where permitted and disclosed.
non_obvious_insight: Incentive budgets buy payment relief, not qualification, and the qualification gap is large. Lennar's Stuart Miller says nearly 50% of visitors cannot immediately qualify, average incentives are about 12% of a $372K price, and buydown costs are rising with rates (https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/17/lennar-len-q3-2026-earnings-call-transcript/). KB Home reports an 18% cancellation rate, an 85% mortgage capture rate and 'minor adjustments' to keep buyers qualified, and buyers 'want to play the market and hope that rates come down' (https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/23/kb-home-kbh-q3-2026-earnings-call-transcript/). Credit-repair vendors have a poor reputation, and lenders have no incentive to coach a borrower for months. A builder paying per closing, the way it pays a broker, is a distribution model none of them have.
first_30_days: Approach 10 regional builders (100-1,000 homes a year) and their affiliated lenders, offering a free 60-day pilot in 1-2 communities. Pull the builder's list of leads that failed pre-qualification in the last 6 months, ask a partner loan officer to tag the failure reason, and run a manual outreach and coaching pass with two HUD-certified housing counselors. Track conversions weekly and sign a success-fee agreement once 3 closings are attributable.

title: Dealer-Fee Decoder for Solar and Home Loans
one_liner: Use the auto F&I trick of hiding the buy-down in the price to expose the hidden 'dealer fee' inside 0% and low-rate solar, HVAC and roofing loans, then sell the evidence to consumer lawyers and the refinance to credit unions.
customer: First: consumer-protection and TILA law firms and legal aid running home-improvement and solar loan cases, at $49 to $149 per decoded loan. Second: credit unions and community banks that pay $150 to $300 per funded takeout loan.
problem: A '0% for 12 months' or '2.99% for 20 years' home-improvement loan is not cheap. The lender charges the contractor a discount or 'dealer fee' that commonly runs into double digits on promotional-rate loans, and the contractor recovers it by inflating the price for financed customers. It's the same mechanic as a dealer's reserve and buy-down in an auto F&I office. The borrower sees a low APR, cannot see the cash price they should have been quoted, and often pays a financed price 15 to 30% above the cash price. Minnesota's attorney general has sued GoodLeap over hidden fees folded into loan amounts, and complaints keep growing. Homeowners left with orphaned systems and no tax credit are a sympathetic and litigable group.
solution: A document-parsing decoder. The homeowner or lawyer uploads the contract, TILA disclosure and any competing cash quote. The tool extracts price, APR, term and any disclosed fee, and estimates the implied cash price and implied finance charge, meaning how much of the price is really interest. It compares this to a regional cash-price benchmark built from scraped quotes, contractor bid sites and permit data. It outputs a plain-language one-pager and a lawyer-grade exhibit for TILA and UDAP claims, then offers a credit-union takeout quote for the true payoff amount.
why_now: The federal residential solar tax credit for homeowner purchases ended after 2025, a wave of installers went bankrupt and left homeowners with loans on systems nobody services, state attorneys general have started suing, and the CFPB's federal enforcement has faded so states and private plaintiffs are the enforcement. Contingency-fee plaintiff firms are already advertising for GoodLeap-type cases and need faster intake screening.
revenue_model: Per-case fee from law firms ($49 to $149), a subscription for high-volume firms ($499 per month), and a bounty from credit unions for each funded refinance or takeout loan. Later, a compliance benchmark sold to honest contractors, to lenders and to regulators.
non_obvious_insight: Consumer advocates attack solar lenders as if the fee were unique to solar. A finance manager knows it is standard structure anywhere a merchant can 'buy down' a rate: the retail price quietly carries the cost. What law firms lack is not the theory but cheap, defensible, per-loan numbers to screen thousands of leads. The cash price counterfactual is the missing piece and the F&I mindset is exactly what tells you where to look for it.
first_30_days: Collect 200 real solar and HVAC loan document sets and cash-vs-financed quote pairs from public complaints, forums and two or three law-firm partners. Build the parser and implied-price model on them. Offer three plaintiff firms with active solar-loan intake 25 free screens each, then charge $99 a case. Meet two credit unions with home-improvement loan programs to agree a bounty for takeouts.

title: Two A.M. Any-Tradition Rites and Interpreter Line
one_liner: A 24/7 dispatch of vetted ritual specialists and death-trained interpreters for families outside the majority faith, sold to hospices and palliative units.
customer: Hospices, hospital palliative units and nursing homes in metros with large immigrant and non-Christian populations. They pay a monthly retainer plus per-dispatch fees.
problem: Most hospice chaplains are generalists trained in a Christian or interfaith pastoral model, and chaplain FTEs are among the first things cut when margins tighten. When an imam, Hindu priest, Buddhist monk, Sikh granthi, Hmong ritual specialist, Orthodox priest, or Native elder is needed, the family often gets the default chaplain, and the ritual windows are short and unforgiving. Some rites happen only before death, others require that the body not be moved or touched for hours, or that someone be present continuously. Standard hospice protocol says 'call the funeral home now.' Language is the second failure. Family members interpret for the patient and quietly soften bad news. In many languages the word 'dying' is unsayable. Interpreter contracts are priced per minute and built for clinic visits, with no death vocabulary or truth-telling norm training.
solution: A dispatch line and app for the hospice chaplain or on-call nurse. It connects to a vetted, paid roster of ritual specialists by tradition and language who can arrive or join by video, plus a small pool of interpreters who have completed a 40-hour end-of-life interpreting course (death vocabulary, family-filtering, cultural norms about naming prognosis). A one-page 'rite card' library is loaded into the hospice's EHR or intranet for each tradition. It gives the practical do's and don'ts: how to position the patient, what not to do to the body, who should not touch it, how long to wait before calling the funeral home, and what the family may ask for. Start with one metro and 4 to 6 traditions.
why_now: AI translation is tempting hospices to cut interpreter budgets, while civil-rights language-access rules (Section 1557 of the ACA as revised in 2024) push toward qualified interpreters and human review of machine translation for critical content. Confirm the current status of those rules. The older-adult population is more foreign-born and religiously diverse than a decade ago, and the unaffiliated 'nones' need secular rituals too. Chaplain staffing is shrinking. Consolidated hospice chains want scalable ways to meet 'emotional and spiritual support' quality measures.
revenue_model: A monthly retainer of $1,500 to $4,000 per hospice or hospital for 24/7 access. Per-dispatch fees ($150 to $300 to the specialist, with a 30 to 40 percent platform margin). Premium per-minute interpreting rates above standard telephone rates. Training and certification revenue from the interpreter course, sold to language-service companies and hospitals. Family fees are not charged.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce thing is not spiritual care in general but time-critical, tradition-specific competence at the exact hour of death, which a generalist chaplain honestly cannot supply. Family interpreters are the largest hidden source of bad-news distortion in end-of-life care. Whoever builds the roster and the interpreter standard owns a moat that AI translation cannot cross, because the value is trust and ritual authority, not words.
first_30_days: Pick one metro where you know the communities (for example Minneapolis–St. Paul for Hmong, Somali and Karen families, or Houston or Queens for a wider mix). Recruit 20 to 25 ritual specialists and interpreters through mosque, temple and community boards, and pay them a small stipend for a 3-hour training on hospice basics. Build the rite-card library with their input. Sign two hospices to a free 60-day pilot on a shared phone number, then convert them to a retainer and use their case counts in a pitch to the next five.

title: Mid-Term Premium True-Down for Shrinking Payrolls
one_liner: Monitor payroll against the estimate on a small business's workers' comp and liability policy, and file mid-term endorsements to cut inflated installments and misclassified codes.
customer: Small businesses with 10-200 employees and volatile payroll (trades, restaurants, staffing, light manufacturing) that already run payroll on Gusto, ADP, Rippling or QuickBooks, reached through CPAs and bookkeepers.
problem: Workers' comp and general liability premiums are priced on estimated payroll and revenue, and only reconciled at year-end audit. When headcount drops, the business keeps paying installments on inflated estimates, financing the insurer, often through premium finance at rising interest. Class-code misclassification (office staff coded as field staff) is also common. Brokers are paid a percentage of premium, so nobody is paid to lower it mid-term.
solution: Connect payroll data, compare actual payroll by class code with the policy estimate each month, generate the carrier endorsement request and support documents, and track the reduced installment schedule. Audit class codes and prepare audit-ready records. Offer optional pay-as-you-go workers' comp placement later.
why_now: Hiring freezes and layoffs are rising as the economy cools. Higher rates raise the cost of premium financing and make cash tighter. Payroll APIs are mature enough to automate the variance check.
revenue_model: 20% of the first-year realized premium reduction, or $49-99 per month SaaS. Partnerships with CPA firms and bookkeepers.
non_obvious_insight: The blocker is incentives, not technology. Brokers earn commission on premium, so no one in the chain is paid to file the endorsement. Downturns make the savings largest exactly when cash is scarcest.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 small businesses through two CPA or bookkeeper networks. Review each policy's declarations page against the last three months of payroll. File endorsements and misclassification challenges by hand, record the realized savings and set pricing at 20% of the first-year benefit.

title: Laid-Off Managers Buy Retiring Owners' Funeral Homes
one_liner: A matchmaker, training cohort and SBA-loan packager that pairs displaced mid-career operators with retiring owners of independent funeral homes, so local homes stay local and the buyers get AI-proof, trust-based work.
customer: Buyers: laid-off director- and VP-level ops, HR, finance and customer-experience people aged 38-55 with severance, savings or a 401(k) rollover for a down payment. Sellers: independent funeral-home owners aged 60+ with no child taking over (NFDA counts 15,401 US funeral homes, about 75% family or privately owned).
problem: Owners have no succession plan, and their realistic exit is a consolidator (SCI, Everstory and others) that dissolves the local name and pushes preneed. White-collar workers hit by the hiring freeze (Amazon cut about 16,000 corporate roles in Jan 2026; information-sector jobs fell 23K in Aug) cannot find durable human-presence work. Licensing rules and deal mechanics make the path opaque.
solution: A 10-week 'Director-Owner Program': state-by-state licensing roadmap (many states let an unlicensed owner run a home if a licensed director-in-charge is employed, but verify each state), a 6-12 month paid apprenticeship placement inside a partner home before closing, FTC Funeral Rule and preneed-trust training, and SBA 7(a) plus seller-note structuring. Add confidential seller listings and matching. After closing, a shared ops kit (software, price-list compliance, vendor rates) and a peer board of owner-operators.
why_now: SCI's Q2'26 results (preneed sales +7%, operating cash flow +43%, volume -1.4%) show value is in pricing and preneed, not volume, so well-run independents are valuable. Cremation is heading to about 82% by 2045, which lowers facility needs. Consumer interest in green options (61.4%) gives new owners a differentiator that legacy owners ignore. Displaced managers are abundant now.
revenue_model: Buyer tuition of about $4,500 (partly deferred to close). Seller-side success fee of 1.5-3% or $15-25K. Deal-packaging fee of about $5K. Owner-community subscription of $199/mo. Later: software and preneed-admin services.
non_obvious_insight: The funeral-home succession gap and the mid-career white-collar glut are the same problem seen from two ends. The best buyer is a people-good operator, not a financier, and consolidators structurally cannot serve either side: they overpay for scale and cannot preserve local identity. It is the ultimate trust job, and AI cannot hold a widow's hand.
first_30_days: Choose two states with friendly licensing and many rural homes. Phone 100 owners aged 60+ via the state funeral-directors association, aiming for 5 signed no-cost 12-month 'successor search' agreements. Recruit the first 10 buyers from laid-off-manager communities (ex-Amazon alumni groups, LinkedIn, Blind) with a $500 refundable screening deposit. Pre-qualify with one SBA lender. Start 1-2 apprenticeships at partner homes.
